1419.prule: No positional rule stated. Stress is described by morpheme/word class (unstressable function morphemes; obligatorily stressed prefixes ré-, dé-, mém, én; every content word has at least one 'stressable' syllable) and is marked lexically with an acute accent on each word cited in isolation; stress placement is stated to distinguish words (refér vs réfer, la vs lá, kúd-kúd vs kud-kúd). The authors' own isolation transcriptions show both final and penultimate stress in disyllabic content words (dimál, lakáz, simíz vs tímid, zárdeṅ, fígir, zóli, túzur, kúma).

1425.dq: Mualang stress is assigned depending on syntactic context, i.e. in isolated words (“word stress”), or on context (“stress beyond the word”). The word stress is assumed as the default, basic one, because it is normally found in citation. If words occur in context, intonational patterns can override this default stress.

1425.heavy: A penultimate syllable whose nucleus is schwa cannot bear stress ('The phoneme /ə/ never occurs in stressed or final syllables'); stress then goes to the ultimate. No reference to vowel length or codas.
1425.prule: Word stress (citation form) is penultimate by default; the penult cannot be stressed if its nucleus is schwa (schwa never occurs in stressed syllables), in which case stress is ultimate. evidence_works.detail: The 1967 phonemic statement gives Muinane 'a two-level pitch system; and... phonemic syllables consisting of a unit of tone placement' (p. 37); 'The suprasegmental phonemes are high tone (marked by ´ over the vowel) and low tone (unmarked)' with 'A tone glide... when contiguous vowels have diverse tones' (p. 42, sec. 5.1); 'There never appears to be contrast, however, between more than two levels' and 'the only pattern found for two-syllable words in isolation is high low', with three-syllable patterns HLH, LHL, HHL, LLH listed (p. 43); the phonemic syllable is 'a unit of potential tone placement consisting of a single vowel with or without preceding consonant' (p. 43, sec. 6.1); 'Both high and low tone occur word initial, medial, and final' (p. 45, sec. 6.5). 1433.prule: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable: 'in these verbs the stress falls on the penultimate syllable. As it does in transitive verbs with an objective suffix'; 'the stress follows the rule: on the penultimate syllable'; 'predictable (penultimate syllable) in an overwhelming majority of words' (Lithgow & Lithgow 1973, pp. 6-8: í-gig 'he laughs', í-kʌlivʌ́tɔw 'he falls', i-gútu-gw 'he pulls me out', í-gut 'he pulls out'). Lithgow 1978 marks the accent on the penult in every polysyllabic noun pattern (kʌ́nig, gʌmʌ́gal, ligúlagʷ, kʌyʌ́mat, tʌnmúnum, muyávig, ʌdkábɔls, pp. 22-24) and on the prefix of one-syllable intransitive stems (ímad, íbas, ígay, p. 24); its p. 31 remark that 'the last vowel of most words is lengthened, and most words end in a consonant... this is a good help in deciding where a word ends' concerns final-vowel length, which it marks separately from the accent (tʌ́ma.n 'father': acute on the penult, length dot on the final vowel). The 1974 dictionary marks stress per entry ('It is essential to stress the right vowel in a word') and its paradigms show the penult in plain forms (alívan 'I speak', námag 'my hand', kákeig 'my leg', gunbunátum 'my house', ákam 'I am eating', ímoum 'he is drinking'; 'For intransitive verbs of one syllable the stress falls on the subject prefix', p. 18). Surface final stress arises in transitive verbs with the zero 3sg object, where the stem-final vowel is elided and the stress stays on the stem syllable (1973 pp. 6-8, 18: verb stem CVCV -> CVC word-finally; i-gút-ø 'he pulls it out' vs í-gut 'he pulls out', ʌ-bɛ́s-ø 'I pierce it' vs á-bas 'I am piercing', b-i-ván-ø 'he will stand on it' vs b-é-van; 1974 p. 14 'For an intransitive verb to become transitive, the stress moves to the final syllable of the stem': ilívan 'he speaks' / iliván 'he says it'; imóm 'he drank it' / ímoum 'he is drinking'), in a few intransitive stems with an underlying final vowel (á-siw 'I enter' / ʌ-síw 'I stay away', ku-síwa-s 'you (pl.) stay away', Lithgow, Lithgow & Bee 1970 p. 17; nasés 'I stay', 1974 p. 17), and in the non-inclusive plural of intimately possessed nouns ('a change in stress in the noun stem', 1974 pp. 10-11: túwan 'his older brother' / tuwán 'his older brothers'; náman 'his hand' / nimém 'our hands, but not yours').

1438.dq: Since metrification is at issue here, some discussion of Naasioi word stress is warranted. Stress normally falls on the second mora of words with three or more moras, as shown in (3) and (4), which suggests a peninitial pattern.
1438.dloc: Brown 2025 section 2.1 'Stress patterns', pp. 4-5; exceptions at fn. 2 (p. 4), sec. 2.3 p. 7 and fn. 8 (p. 12); OPD p. 2 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)'.
1438.heavy: Long vowels are bimoraic ('long vowels are treated as if they were sequences; that is, each vowel portion counts as a stress bearing unit'); codas are not ('there is no evidence to suggest that coda consonants are moraic in the system, because stress does not shift as a function of the presence or absence of codas').
1438.dflt: second syllable (= second mora) in words of 3+ moras; first syllable in bimoraic (CV.CV(C)) disyllables
1438.prule: Predictable, non-contrastive word stress on the PENINITIAL MORA: the second mora from the left edge in words of three or more moras; long vowels count as two stress-bearing units (each vowel portion a mora), coda consonants (nasals, glottal stop) are weightless. Nonfinality: bimoraic words (light-light disyllables) stress the first mora instead. In syllable terms: stress the first syllable if it contains a long vowel (taáβi), otherwise the second syllable (panóko, baɾáama, kakúu); CV.CV(C) disyllables are initial-stressed (báɾeŋ). One stress per word, no secondary stress (acoustically verified). Hurd's 1992 OPD states the same rule in vowel=syllable terms: 'first syllable of two syllable words and the second syllable of longer words'.
1438.srule: None. Brown 2025 finds a single stress per word and no secondary stress: in words of five or more moras there is a stress on the second mora and no other detectable pitch peaks or durational differences (e.g. [otómemoa]); Hurd & Hurd 1970 likewise mention none.

1439.heavy: Heavy = CVV and (nonfinal) CVC; final consonants are extrametrical/licensed to the prosodic word, 'rendering heavy syllables CVC, CVVC, and CVCC to light CV, heavy CVV, and CVC respectively'; light = CV (and word-final CVC).
1439.prule: (1) Primary stress on a final superheavy syllable (CVCC or CVVC; final C is extrametrical so final CVC counts as light, final CVVC/CVCC as heavy); (2) otherwise on the rightmost heavy syllable (CVV or nonfinal CVC), 'up to the antepenultimate' (e.g. (ˈmar)(ti.ba)h 'mattress', mu(ˈdar)(rɪ.sa)h 'teacher F'); (3) a lone heavy is stressed wherever it is (ga(ˈlam) 'pen'); (4) if no heavy syllable, stress the leftmost (initial) light syllable ((ˈbala) 'problem', k(ˈta.ba)ha 'he wrote it').
1439.srule: One secondary stress on the first or second heavy syllable from the left edge of the word, unless it would clash with the primary on the rightmost heavy ((ˌmus)(ta.wa)(ˈja:)t 'levels', (ˌdar)ra(ˈsat)ni 'he taught me'; no secondary in jɪ.(ʕal)(ˈlɪm)hum, NoClash); heavy syllables only, not iterative.

1443.tone: Both primaries analyse Namuyi as tonal. Pavlík 2017 (NMZ): each word carries a distinctive tone, 6 surface contours, at most ~4 tonemes, tone unstable under intonation and levelled in compounds; the thesis never mentions stress or accent in a prosodic sense (full-text search). Nishida 2013 (Dzolo/Mianning): 'Nàmùyì is a tone language with different pitch variation on a syllable or phonological word to convey meaning... producing lexically contrastive tones' (p.39); 4 tonemes (H, Falling, Rising, L; tonemes 1-2 merging to a 3-tone system in the author's data), default tone L, tones deleted from non-initial syllables, suffixes take pitch from the stem ('word tone language', p.47-48), tonemes restated as placement of an 'accentual nucleus' (F = /'oo/, R = /o'o/); he cites his own 2005 talk 'On pitch accent in the Namuyi language'. Nishida additionally gives a weak, hedged root-initial word-stress tendency with some final-stress words (sec. 2.6, p.49; quoted above). Caveat: that stress/intonation prose is visibly templated from a Gurung description (heading '2.6 Stress assignment in Gurung', 'we can call Gurung a word tone language', 'The greatest change in Gurung phonology'), so it carries reduced independent weight.

1444.tone: Reachable modern sources describe Nandi/Kalenjin purely in tonal terms: lexical tone (H, L, rising, high-falling, low-falling; rising an allotone of H on long vowels) plus tonal case marking (nominative = lexical tones replaced by a fixed pattern), Creider & Creider 1989: 23, 42-43 as carried by the open Pressbooks profile; Creider 1982 is a monograph on Nandi nominal tonology (Dimmendaal 2012 sec. 4.1); Lodge 1995: 31 (Lingua 96) states outright 'Kalenjin is a tone language, but whether the tonal system interacts with the harmony system is not clear, so I have not included tonal markings in the transcriptions'. None of the reachable modern texts states a word-stress rule. Hollis 1909, writing before tonal analysis, heard no consistent word accent ('all syllables are accentuated alike, a slight stress being perhaps laid on the penultimate') and noted raised pitch in interrogatives - consistent with a tone language without contrastive stress.

1445.tone: Heath describes a full Dogon-type tone system (lexical stem melodies plus grammatically controlled tone overlays, ch. 3.7) and explicitly says 'Stress and accent patterns... are not relevant to Nanga' (3.6). The only stress-like notion is a 'trochaic bias' in 3.2.2: segmental rules treat the medial syllable of CvCvCv stems as metrically weak (short high vowel, syncope-prone); 'prosodic weight' (light = two vocalic moras vs heavy = more) conditions some tonal/vocalic processes in verb morphology, not a stress position. The word 'stress' otherwise occurs only re English emphatic stress (p. ~ch.10) and 'distressed cow'.
